info.bio:
Johnny Cash, nacido John Ray Cash (26 de febrero de 1932 - 12 de septiembre de 2003) fue un cantautor estadounidense de country, gospel, rock and roll y rockabilly. Fue uno de los máximos representantes de la música country, aunque creó su propio subgénero musical.

Cash fue conocido por su profunda voz, por el característico sonido boom-chick-a-boom de su banda de acompañamiento, los Tennessee Three y, por vestir ropa oscura, lo que le valió el apodo de «El Hombre de Negro» («The Man in Black»).

scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Conflicting Accounts of Million Dollar Quartet Participation (1956)
podcast.body: Accounts vary widely regarding Johnny Cash's involvement in the legendary Million Dollar Quartet session on December 4, 1956. Cash himself claimed he was the first to arrive and the last to leave, watching his friends record and staying for the entire jam session. Other versions suggest he arrived mid-session to collect a royalty check, sang a few songs off-tape, and then left for Christmas shopping. Yet another account implies Sam Phillips, seeking publicity for Sun Records' biggest act, called Cash, along with journalists and photographers, implying Cash only appeared for a photo opportunity before departing. "Every single account of what became known as the million dollar quartet session disagrees as to how much, ever at all, Johnny Cash participated in the proceedings."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Post-1956 Career Shift
podcast.body: After December 4, 1956, Johnny Cash, along with Carl Perkins, increasingly moved towards country music and away from rockabilly. This date is considered a significant border in rock and roll history, marking a period before rock and roll became the dominant genre. "They both moved increasingly towards country music, and away from rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Shift to Country Music Promotion (1956)
podcast.body: By December 1956, Johnny Cash began to be actively promoted as a country singer rather than a rock and roller. This shift coincided with the decline of the first wave of rockabilly. "Johnny Cash had started to be promoted as a country singer, rather than a rock and roller."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Singing Style on Million Dollar Quartet Tapes (1956)
podcast.body: On the Million Dollar Quartet jam session tapes, which were recorded on a single microphone and released in the 1980s, Johnny Cash is difficult to hear. He claimed he was positioned furthest from the microphone and sang in a higher register than usual to match the keys comfortable for the other three musicians (Elvis Presley, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Carl Perkins). "Cash always said that he was there, just the furthest from the microphone, and that he was singing in a higher register than normal, because he was trying to sing in the keys that were comfortable for the other three."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: The Johnny Cash Show (1969-1971)
podcast.body: Debuting in June 1969, just a week before "Hee Haw," The Johnny Cash Show featured a diverse array of stars, often including guests like Bob Hope to satisfy ABC executives. Despite its cross-section of musical artists that went beyond just country, the show was canceled in 1971 as part of CBS's "rural purge." "The Johnny Cash show went on the air a week earlier in June 1969. Like Glenn Campbell, Johnny Cash had a wide variety of stars on his show."

podcast.body: Johnny Cash was 71 years old and in very poor health when the video for "Hurt" was filmed. He died seven months after the video was shot. "Cash was 71 at the time, the video was shot and he was in very poor health."

podcast.title: Army Service Intercepting Soviet Messages
podcast.body: As a 19-year-old Air Force recruit in the army, Johnny Cash spent three years stationed in Germany. During this time, his duties involved intercepting Soviet messages that were transmitted in Morse code to their combat aircraft. "he spent three years in Germany intercepting Soviet messages sent in Morse code to their combat aircraft."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Facts in 30 Minutes: 2020 Edition

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – American Flag Requirement
podcast.body: Johnny Cash, known as "the man in black" and a simple individual, had one non-negotiable item in his rider: an American flag that had to be displayed in full view of the audience during his performances. "The one thing he would not skip on was an American flag that had to be displayed in full view of the audience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Backstage Rider

podcast.title: Birth Name and Name Change
podcast.body: Johnny Cash's birth name was J.R. Cash, initials chosen by his parents who disagreed on a full name. When he joined the Air Force, he was not allowed to use just initials, so he changed his name to John R. Cash. He adopted "Johnny Cash" only after becoming a professional musician, still without a middle name, just the middle initial. "His parents apparently had a disagreement over what their son's name should be, and so rather than give him full names, they just gave him initials."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Career Resurgence with Rick Rubin (2000s)
podcast.body: In the early 2000s, Johnny Cash's career had stagnated, but a connection with producer Rick Rubin led to the concept of Cash covering contemporary songs in his unique style. This collaboration revitalized his career, turning him into an "alternative hero" and solidifying his image as "the original man in black." "But then he connected with producer Rick Rubin and came up with the idea of Cash covering contemporary songs in his own way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 9 Great Alt-Rock Cover Songs

podcast.title: Cash Home and "Hurt" Video Props
podcast.body: The house featured in the "Hurt" video was Johnny Cash's home for 30 years and had become a museum in Hendersonville, Tennessee, before it tragically burned to the ground in 2007. The chair in which Cash is seen sitting in the video is on permanent display behind glass at the Jody Cash Museum in Nashville. "The house in the video, the Cash home for 30 years in the museum in Hendersonville, Tennessee, was in really rough shape. It burned to the ground in 2007."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 9 Great Alt-Rock Cover Songs

podcast.title: Close Friendship with Carl and Clayton Perkins
podcast.body: Despite his resentment towards Sam Phillips' perceived favoritism of Carl Perkins, Cash became close friends with Carl. He grew even closer to Carl's wayward brother, Clayton Perkins, whose juvenile sense of humor appealed to Cash. "The two became close friends though Cash became even closer with Clayton Perkins, Carl's wayward brother, who had a juvenile sense of humour that appealed to Cash."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Collaborator with Grady Martin
podcast.body: Johnny Cash is mentioned as one of the artists for whom session guitarist Grady Martin played on recordings. "Grady was a session guitarist in Nashville who played on hundreds of recordings for people like Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and even Buddy Holly."

podcast.title: Commanding Presence
podcast.body: Sam Phillips noted Johnny Cash's commanding presence, distinguishing him from Elvis's charisma, Halem Wolff's profundity, and Jerry Lee Lewis's natural talent and obsession. "Johnny Cash had the most commanding presence."

podcast.title: Complex Relationship with Religious Themes
podcast.body: Despite singing about religion, Johnny Cash also incorporated themes of personal failings, such as cheating on his wife, into his music. This complexity makes country music, as a genre, difficult to recommend wholesale to religious audiences but also keeps it interesting. "Sure, Johnny Cash sang about religion, but he also talked about cheating on his wife."

podcast.title: Contract with Sun Records
podcast.body: When the contract was drawn up, only Johnny Cash was officially signed to Sun Records, as Sam Phillips did not want to be tied to the other two musicians (Luther Perkins and Marshall Grant). Despite this, Cash split the money with them, either in a 40-30-30 split or an entirely equal split, according to different sources. "When the contract was drawn up the only person who was actually signed to son was Cash."

podcast.title: Country Marketing Shift
podcast.body: Initially associated with the rockabilly scene, Johnny Cash, despite continuing to have hits, was progressively marketed as a country music star following the decline of the white rockabilly movement by late 1956. "Johnny Cash would have more hits, but he would increasingly be marketed as a country music star."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Covered Nick Lowe's Tracks
podcast.body: Johnny Cash is mentioned as one of the artists who took Nick Lowe's tracks and turned them into hits, highlighting Lowe's songwriting prowess. Cash's connection to Lowe was also through family, as he was Lowe's father-in-law. "Nick Lowe... had a number of his tracks turned into hits by other artists like Elvis Costello and Johnny Cash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Power Pop

podcast.title: Departure from Sun Records
podcast.body: Johnny Cash, along with Carl Perkins, left Sun Records around the same time Roy Orbison sought to terminate his contract. Phillips suspected collusion, which was accurate, as the three artists shared concerns about Phillips' royalty payments, business transparency, and focus on new acts. "This was at almost exactly the same time that both Johnny Cash and Carl Perkins left Sun records, and he suspected a degree of collusion between the three men, and he wasn't wrong in his suspicion."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Departure from Sun Records
podcast.body: Johnny Cash was in a situation similar to Karl Perkins, where his records were being produced by Jack Clement. Although Cash was writing some of his best material, Clement was insisting he record songs Clement had written, such as "Ballad of a Teenage Queen." This frustration, evident from his mid-November 1957 recording of Clement's song, led Cash, along with Perkins, to agree with Columbia Records on November 1, 1957, to record for them once their Sun contracts expired. "Cash was in a similar situation to Perkins."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Dispute with Sam Phillips over "I Walk the Line" Tempo
podcast.body: Johnny Cash fiercely debated with Sam Phillips about the tempo of "I Walk the Line." Cash envisioned it as a slow, plaintive ballad, while Phillips insisted on a faster, rock and roll tempo for commercial appeal. Phillips ultimately released the faster version, devastating Cash initially, but its massive commercial success led Cash to re-evaluate his opinion. "Cash walked out convinced that Phillips would see reason and released the slower version. He was devastated to find that Phillips had released the faster version."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Dissatisfaction with Sam Phillips
podcast.body: Johnny Cash, like Carl Perkins, was strongly considering moving to another record label due to dissatisfaction with the way Sam Phillips was promoting his work. "Perkins was increasingly dissatisfied with the way Sam Phillips was promoting his work, and like Johnny Cash was strongly considering moving to another label."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Early Musical Ambition and Gospel Roots
podcast.body: Cash was determined to become a famous singer despite not knowing how. Initially, he and his band mostly performed white gospel songs, music he loved. He had a religious experience as a child when his elder brother, who wanted to be a priest, died after a deathbed vision of heaven and hell, inspiring Cash to become a gospel singer in tribute. "Cash had had a religious experience as a kid when his elder brother, who had wanted to become a priest, had died, and had had a deathbed vision of heaven and hell, and Cash wanted to become a gospel singer to pay tribute to his brother while also indulging his own love of music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Early Rock and Roll Star
podcast.body: Johnny Cash is cited as one of the major stars of the early rock and roll era, a romantic figure of legend who is well-documented in many books, in contrast to other important but lesser-known artists of the period. "While you won't find much out there on a lot of truly important artists, you can find out enough about Elvis and Ray Charles and Johnny Cash and Little Richard and Chuck Berry in the rest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Encounter with Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Johnny Cash, along with Luther Perkins and Marshall Grant, went to see Elvis, Scotty, and Bill perform on the back of a flatbed truck. Cash, then 22, was worried he was too old to become a star compared to the teenage Elvis. He later spoke with Scotty Moore, who advised him to contact Sam Phillips at Sun Records. "Cash was immediately worried, Elvis was clearly a teenager, and Cash himself was a grown man of 22."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Featured in Apple Commercials
podcast.body: Johnny Cash's music has been featured in Apple's commercial campaigns, showcasing the tech giant's broad selection of iconic artists across different genres for its iPod and iPhone advertisements.

podcast.title: First American to Learn of Stalin's Death
podcast.body: While serving in the military, Johnny Cash was the radio operator who intercepted and decoded the Russian transmissions announcing Stalin's death, making him the very first American to receive this information. "he'd been the very first American to learn that Stalin had died as he'd been the radio operator who'd intercepted and decoded the Russian transmissions about it."

srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Grammy Recognition for Liner Notes
podcast.body: Although the Grammy Award for Best Liner Notes predominantly recognized classical recordings, collections, and anthologies, several individual Johnny Cash albums were noted for receiving this recognition, indicating the quality of the textual content accompanying his releases. "several individual-jody cash albums were recognized."

srcs.episode: Digital Debris  Part 3: Liner Notes

podcast.title: Honky Tonk vs. Rockabilly
podcast.body: Johnny Cash, along with Elvis Presley, is contrasted with Hank Williams regarding the direction of Country music. While Williams popularized a more traditional Honky Tonk sound, Cash pursued a more rockabilly-oriented style, achieving his initial successes after Williams' death. "A diferencia de otros músicos que llevarían el contri hacia un sonido más roca-bili, como Johnny Cage o Elvis Presley, quienes conseguirán sus primeros éxitos tras la muerte de Williams."

podcast.title: Influence on Tom Yorke
podcast.body: During the recording sessions for "Okay Computer," Tom Yorke found himself "entranced with some old Johnny Cash records," indicating a musical influence or creative interest at the time. "Meanwhile Tom York found himself in trance with some old Johnny Cash records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Radiohead - A History: Part 2

podcast.title: Influenced by Hank Williams
podcast.body: Johnny Cash is mentioned as one of the musicians who followed the path laid out by Hank Williams, highlighting Williams' significant influence on the Country genre and the emerging rock and roll. "trazando un camino que seguirán músicos como Johnny Cash, Dolip Arton o William Nelson."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El genio roto del country: La leyenda de Hank Williams

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Blue Suede Shoes"
podcast.body: While touring with Carl Perkins and Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash shared an anecdote about a fellow serviceman, a black man named C.V. Wright, who referred to his military-issue shoes as "blue suede shoes." Cash suggested this phrase as a potential song idea to Perkins, which eventually led to the creation of the iconic hit. "Cash remembered a fellow serviceman, a black man named CV Wright, had referred to his service issue shoes as blue swed shoes, and he told Perkins that he should write a song about that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Lifelong Fan of Miles Travis
podcast.body: Johnny Cash became a lifelong fan of Miles Travis, the writer of Tennessee Ernie Ford's hit song "Sixteen Tons," which Cash loved when it came out. The imagery in "Sixteen Tons" likely influenced Cash's songwriting for "I Walk the Line." "he made Cash a lifelong fan of his writer, Miles Travis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Management by Bob Neal and Promotion as Rock and Roller
podcast.body: Johnny Cash followed Elvis Presley's career path, being managed by Elvis's first proper manager, Bob Neal, and securing a regular slot on the Louisiana Hayride. This led to Cash being promoted as a rock and roll star alongside Carl Perkins, which broadened his appeal beyond country audiences and contributed to his long-term career success, notably his comeback with the American Recording series decades later. "He was managed by Elvis's first proper manager Bob Neal and he was given a regular slot on the Louisiana Hayride, the country music radio show that Elvis had built his reputation on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Marriage Troubles and Move to Columbia
podcast.body: Despite writing movingly about maintaining his marriage, Johnny Cash's marriage was falling apart. He began to consider moving to a major label, like Elvis Presley had, and was soon signed to Columbia Records, where he would spend most of his career. "His life was in turmoil the marriage that he had written so movingly about trying to keep together was falling apart and he was beginning to think that he would do better doing as Elvis had and moving to a major label soon he would be signed to Columbia the label where he would spend almost all his career."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Million Dollar Quartet Participant
podcast.body: Johnny Cash was present during the famous Million Dollar Quartet sessions when Elvis Presley continually raved about Jackie Wilson, then a singer with Billy Ward and the Dominoes. "In the famous million dollar quartet tapes, you can hear Elvis raving about Wilson to Johnny Cash, Karl Perkins, and Jerry Lee Lewis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Move to Memphis and Band Formation (Age 22)
podcast.body: After returning to the US from his Air Force stint in Germany at age 22, Cash married and moved to Memphis to be near his brother. His brother introduced him to Luther Perkins and Marshall Grant, with whom he started playing music. "After returning to the US from his stint in the Air Force in Germany, aged 22, Cash got married and moved to Memphis to be near his brother."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Musical Parent
podcast.body: Johnny Cash is mentioned as a musical parent, with his daughter Rosanne also having a musical career. "Well, Johnny Cash and daughter Rosanne."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musical Offspring

podcast.title: O.B. McClinton Impression
podcast.body: O.B. McClinton used Johnny Cash as an example in his live shows to illustrate the difference between country and rhythm and blues. He would sing the same song first in the style of Johnny Cash and then in the style of Muddy Waters. "I illustrate the difference between country and rhythm and blues by singing the same song as if I were Johnny Cash and then Muddy Waters."

podcast.title: Overton Park Shell Concert (June 1)
podcast.body: Johnny Cash performed at the Overton Park Shell in Memphis on Friday, June 1, at 8 p.m., as part of a country rock and roll show. He shared the stage with Kyle Perkins, Warren Smith, Roy Orbison, and Eddie Bond and the Stumpers. "There'll be Johnny Cash in the Tennessee too with Cry Cry Cry and Folsom Prison Blues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Sun Career
podcast.body: After leaving Sun Records for Columbia, Johnny Cash went on to achieve greater success. "While Cash would go on to have greater success at Columbia, Perkins wouldn't, and ironically it was possible that he had had one more opportunity to have a hit follow-up to Blue Swade Shoes at Sun, and he passed on it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Rejection of Gospel Music by Sam Phillips
podcast.body: During an audition, Sam Phillips expressed disinterest in releasing gospel music, stating he had no sales success with it and wanted something more commercial. While an urban legend suggests Phillips told Cash to "go home and sin, then come back with a song I can sell," Cash denied this, but he did take the hint and began writing secular songs. "Phillips liked their sound, but explained that he wasn't particularly interested in putting out gospel music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Religious Background
podcast.body: Johnny Cash was a deeply religious man, though he was not brought up in the Assembly of God Pentecostal tradition, unlike Elvis Presley and Jerry Lee Lewis. "Both Elvis and Jerry Lee were brought up in the assembly of God, a Pentecostal holy roller church, which we'll talk more about when we get to an episode on Jerry Lee himself. But that meant they shared even more of a religious culture than they did with cash or perkins, both of whom were deeply religious men, but neither of whom were brought up in that particular tradition."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Resentment Towards Jerry Lee Lewis
podcast.body: Johnny Cash became friends with Jerry Lee Lewis during a tour with Carl Perkins and Wanda Jackson, but he also started to resent Lewis's status as Sam Phillips's "new golden boy" and plotted ways to leave their contract with Sun Records to avoid being overshadowed. "Perkins and Cash were already starting to resent the fact that Jerry Lee was clearly Sam Phillips's new golden boy and plotting ways to get out of their contract with Son and go somewhere that they'd not be overshadowed by this wild kid."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Resentment Towards Sam Phillips' Favoritism
podcast.body: Johnny Cash resented Sam Phillips for seemingly treating him as less important after Phillips signed Carl Perkins, believing Phillips was only interested in his new star and wouldn't promote Cash's records. This pattern of perceived favoritism would recur with Phillips' new discoveries and contributed to the eventual downfall of Sun Records as artists left for other labels. "Cash resented the way that he was being treated by Phillips as being less important than Perkins."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Rockabilly to Pure Country
podcast.body: Following the disappearance of rockabilly from the charts, Johnny Cash was among the musicians who moved into "pure country" music. "or into pure country, like Johnny Cash."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Solo Audition for Sam Phillips
podcast.body: After failing to reach Sam Phillips by phone, Johnny Cash went to see Phillips alone for his first audition. Phillips was immediately impressed by Cash's dignified bearing, presence, and gravitas, seeing him as having the makings of a star. "Phillips was immediately impressed by Cash's bearing and presence. He was taller and more dignified than most of the people who came into audition for Phillips."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Sun Records Success after Elvis
podcast.body: Johnny Cash generated "massive hits" for Sun Records after Elvis Presley's departure, a success largely attributed to the financial influx the label received from the Elvis-RCA deal. "It was able to generate massive hits for Karl Perkins and Johnny Cash after Elvis left, but that's only because of the cash the label was able to make from the Elvis deal."

podcast.title: Unhelpful Advice to Orbison
podcast.body: Johnny Cash gave Roy Orbison Sam Phillips' phone number and advised him to say Cash had sent him, which initially resulted in Phillips slamming the phone down. Cash also suggested Orbison sing in a lower register and change his name, advice Orbison never took. "Cash gave Orbison the phone number for Sam Phillips and told him to tell Phillips that Cash had sent him. He also advised Orbison that if he wanted to have any success as a musician he should probably start singing in a lower register and maybe change his name."

podcast.title: Voice Description
podcast.body: Even as a young man, Johnny Cash's voice was described as if "carved out of rock and imbued with the spirit of an Old Testament prophet." He didn't have a huge range but possessed an astonishingly sonorous, resonant bass-baritone that commanded attention. "Cash never had a huge range, but his voice had a sonority to it that was quite astonishing, a resonant bass baritone that demanded you pay attention to what it had to say."

xref.body: Throughout his six-decade career, Ben Dorsi worked for numerous prominent artists, starting with Hank Thompson, then a young Elvis Presley, followed by Johnny Cash, Patsy Cline, Kris Kristofferson, Merle Haggard, and Willie Nelson. xref.body: Nick Lowe was Johnny Cash's father-in-law, a notable personal connection that links him to another iconic figure in music history, and also explains how Cash came to cover some of Lowe's tracks. "Johnny Cash by the way was Nick's father-in-law."

xref.title: Flea's Studio Work
xref.body: Flea is considered one of the greatest bass players in the world, leading to his hiring as a studio musician for diverse artists including Alanis Morissette, Mick Jagger, and Johnny Cash. He also played bass on Young MC's hit "Busta Move." "He is so good that he has been hired as a studio musician by everyone from Alannis Morse set to Mick Jagger to Johnny Cash."

xref.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a queer Black woman from Cotton Plant, Arkansas, is widely called the "Godmother of rock and roll." She was a pioneering guitarist who transitioned to the electric guitar, revered by figures like Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Chuck Berry for her influential bridge between gospel blues and swing music. "A lot of people will point to sister Rosetta Thar, a guitarist who graduated to the electric guitar and has been called the Godmother of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

xref.title: Influences During Okay Computer Sessions
xref.body: During the recording of what would become "Okay Computer," Jonny Greenwood was heavily influenced by Pink Floyd, listening to their old albums and watching performance films. Tom Yorke, meanwhile, was entranced by old Johnny Cash records. "Johnny Greenwood was into a big pink void trip at the time, fortunate to listen to all these old albums and demanding that they watch old pink void performance films."

xref.title: Musical Uniqueness and Influences
xref.body: The Happy Mondays developed a completely unique sound, deliberately avoiding sounding like any one artist because they listened to a vast range of genres and artists, from Johnny Cash and Sly & The Family Stone to the Sex Pistols, The Band, William Ellison, The Rolling Stones, and The Beatles. This eclectic listening, coupled with their own perceived lack of traditional musical proficiency, resulted in a distinctive groove. "We just listened to everything. We didn't try it at the anyone, because we couldn't be, we weren't good enough."

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Guitar Heroes

xref.title: Session Guitarist on Iconic Recordings
xref.body: Grady Martin was a prolific session guitarist in Nashville, contributing to hundreds of recordings for prominent artists such as Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, and Buddy Holly. His work as a session musician placed him at the heart of many significant musical developments. "Grady was a session guitarist in Nashville who played on hundreds of recordings for people like Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash and even Buddy Holly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: Songwriting Influence
xref.body: Nick Lowe is a highly influential songwriter, not only having hit singles of his own but also seeing several of his tracks become hits for other artists, including Elvis Costello and Johnny Cash. His talent is recognized by contemporary musicians, with Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys citing him as a favorite songwriter. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."
